name: Tigrinya
family: Afro-Asiatic, Semitic, South Semitic (Ethiosemitic), North Ethiopic
variety: Tigrinya of Eritrea and Tigray in its written standard form (central, Asmara-type pronunciation)
sources: Kogan, Leonid E. (1997). Tigrinya. In Robert Hetzron (ed.), The Semitic Languages. London: Routledge.
Leslau, Wolf (1941). Documents tigrigna (éthiopien septentrional): grammaire et textes. Paris: Klincksieck.
Shosted, Ryan K. & Rose, Sharon (2011). Affricating ejective fricatives: the case of Tigrinya. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 41(1): 41-65.
Kingston, John (1985). The phonetics and phonology of the timing of oral and glottal events. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley.
Fre Woldu, Kiros (1985). The perception and production of Tigrinya stops. Uppsala University.
Buckley, Eugene (1994). Tigrinya vowel features and vowel coalescence. University of Pennsylvania Working Papers in Linguistics 1.
Buckley, Eugene (1997). Against vowel length in Tigrinya. Studies in African Linguistics 26(1).
contrasts: three-way laryngeal contrast in stops and affricates: voiceless, voiced, ejective
consonant gemination, lexical and grammatical, not shown in the script
seven vowels; the first-order vowel, written ä and given here as /ɐ/, is also transcribed /ə/
/p/ and /v/ occur in loanwords only, /pʼ/ is rare
allophony: /k/ and /kʼ/ are spirantised after a vowel when they are not geminate: [x] and an ejective fricative or affricate that is often uvular, [xʼ]~[χʼ]; the labialised velars behave the same way. The script writes the spirantised forms with separate letters (ኸ, ቐ)
/b/ is [β] after a vowel when not geminate

ejective stops are of the tense type: the release is followed by a silent interval that comes from the glottal closure, so the time from release to voicing is long (Kingston 1985); this silence after the release is the most reliable cue that separates them from the pulmonic stops (Fre Woldu 1985)
next to the pharyngeals and glottals /ɐ/ is lowered to [a]
single /r/ is a tap, geminate /rr/ a trill
/ɨ/ is mostly epenthetic; at the end of a word the epenthetic vowel is [i]
phonotactics: no consonant clusters within a syllable: a sequence of three consonants is broken by an epenthetic vowel
word-final clusters are followed by an epenthetic [i]
pharyngeal and glottal consonants are never geminate
spirantised [x xʼ] occur only after a vowel and only when single
labialised velars do not occur before the rounded vowels /u o/

stress.rule: Stress is neither contrastive nor salient and no fixed position is established; prominence goes with heavy syllables, above all those closed by a geminate.

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none caused by stress; the central vowel /ɨ/ is short and may be dropped where the syllable structure allows
rhythm.notes: The class is an impressionistic label based on the weak stress and simple syllables; no rhythm-metric study is cited.

length.notes: Geminates contrast with single consonants; Buckley (1997) argues that vowel length is not contrastive. No duration ratio is given here.

intonation.declarative: gradual declination with a fall at the end; the verb is final
intonation.yes_no_question: question particle (-do attached to the questioned word) or a final rise
intonation.wh_question: prominence on the question word, falling end
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of non-final clauses
intonation.notes: Tigrinya intonation is little studied; these settings are provisional.

phonation: ejective stops, affricates and fricative (glottalic egressive airstream)
pharyngeal consonants colour the neighbouring vowels

problems: The pharyngeal /ħ/ (ሐ series) is sent to the phoneme X, the uvular fricative [χ]; the ti table has no pharyngeal ħ although the Arabic table has one. ሓደ gives [χadə].
The spirantised ejective (ቐ series, [xʼ]~[χʼ]) is the plain uvular stop q: ቐይሕ gives [qəjɨx].
ጸ and ፀ are the plain affricate [ts], not the ejective /sʼ/ [tsʼ].
Gemination is never produced (the script does not write it): ትግርኛ has a single [ɲ].
Every sixth-order letter inside a word is given the vowel ɨ: ትግርኛ gives [tɨɡɨrɨɲa] for [tɨɡrɨɲɲa], ክልተ gives [kɨlɨtə] for [kɨltə].
No stress rule is set for ti, so the default penultimate stress applies and often lands on an inserted ɨ (kɨlˈɨtə).
Only k` uses an ejective recording; p`, t` and tS` use unaspirated plosive samples after a pause.
The rules were copied from Amharic (the headers of ti_rules and ti_list still say Amharic) and the first-order vowel is the Amharic schwa.
good: b is lenited to [β] between vowels
ejective p, t, tʃ and k are separate phonemes from the plain stops

notes: No published formant or voice onset time figures are given because none could be checked. Shosted & Rose (2011) and Kingston (1985) are the instrumental sources for the ejectives.
